title: Goblin Tumble and the Peculiar Treasure
markdown:
Gather ‘round, you lot, and lean in, because this is the tale of Goblin Tumble and his remarkably opinionated rat, Pickle! You know Tumble – the one with the ears that practically hum when he’s got a zany idea buzzing in his noggin. And Pickle! Ah, Pickle. He’s less a pet, more a furry, four-legged advisor with an exceptional nose for trouble – and cheese, of course. Pickle’s whiskers twitch with more wisdom than most wizards!

Now, Tumble lived way, way up in the jagged peaks of the Whispering Mountains. They looked like giant, grumpy teeth trying to chomp the sky. And the wind there? It didn’t just whistle! It sang opera, told ghost stories, and sometimes, if you listened really closely, you could hear it complaining about the neighbours. It was enough to make your knees go wobbly like overcooked jelly! And scattered about, like forgotten sprinkles on a giant, nature-made cake, were tiny, impossibly perched observatories. They looked like bird nests glued to the very tips of mountains, forever snooping at the vast, glittering expanse of stars.

And it was here, on a particularly Tuesdayish afternoon – you know, the kind of day that feels like a Monday wearing a silly, mismatched hat and still hasn’t had its morning yawn – that Tumble found himself in a pickle… or rather, Pickle found him in a pickle! And Pickle, a rat who knew what he liked, hated being in pickles. Unless it was a dill pickle. Then he was very interested.

His coin pouch, usually a jiggling treasure trove of forgotten pebbles, a shiny button or two, and the occasional dried-up pea, was as empty as a ghost’s lunchbox. And his tummy? Oh, his tummy was staging a full-blown rebellion! It was rumbling with the ferocity of a thousand hungry grubs throwing a noisy party. He needed coins. Proper, clinky, supper-securing coins that smelled faintly of adventure and baked potatoes. But admitting he was as broke as a broken bauble, or a goblin who’d lost his favourite digging spoon? Never! Tumble was far too inventive, far too Tumble-ish for that kind of embarrassing admission.

‘Right then, Pickle,’ Tumble declared, puffing out his chest so his patched-up tunic strained like a tightrope walker’s shoelaces. ‘Operation: Magnificent Meal is a GO!’ He punctuated this with a rather dramatic flourish of his arms, nearly knocking Pickle off his perch.

Pickle, a sleek, intelligent rat with eyes like polished obsidian beads, gave a tiny, almost imperceptible sigh. He’d heard this preamble before. It usually meant a wild goose chase involving peculiar clues and a lot of Tumble’s optimistic grunting.

Tumble unfurled a map. Now, this wasn’t just any map. Oh no! This map belonged to his Great-Uncle Gribble, a goblin of questionable sanity, spectacular taste in mismatched socks (he once wore one with polka dots and another with a picture of a grumpy badger), and an uncanny ability to get lost even in his own kitchen. This map was a masterpiece of goblin cartography: covered in smudges that looked suspiciously like dried berry juice, cryptic scribbles that might have been bird droppings or secret codes, and smelling faintly of burnt toast and the lingering scent of regret from a past failed experiment. It was supposed to lead to the ‘Glimmering Hoard of the High Peaks,’ a treasure trove of… well, Tumble wasn’t entirely sure what. But it sounded expensive enough to buy him several suppers, and maybe even a new hat.

‘According to this,’ Tumble tapped a particularly enthusiastic swirl of ink with a muddy fingernail, ‘the treasure lies… “three paces east of the sighing stone, beneath the eye that never blinks.”’

‘A “sighing stone”?’ Pickle squeaked, his delicate whiskers twitching like tiny antennae picking up a peculiar signal. ‘Does it require a therapist, or just a good breeze?’

‘Precisely!’ Tumble grinned, already striding off with the determined gait of a goblin on a mission. ‘The map is technically correct, of course. Great-Uncle Gribble insisted on that with a stern, sock-mismatched finger wag. The emotional helpfulness, however, is where it gets… interpretive.’

Interpretive was a very polite word for utterly baffling. They trekked for ages, scrambling over rocks and ducking under ancient, gnarled branches that looked like skeletal fingers reaching out. They found a stone, yes. It was grey, lump-shaped, and looked profoundly bored. And when the wind, which was feeling particularly whimsical that day, blew through a tiny, whispering crack in its surface, it made a sound remarkably like a weary sigh. So far, so good! Pickle even gave it a little nod of approval. But the ‘eye that never blinks’? Now that was a puzzle worthy of a thousand Gribble-coins.

They searched high and low. Tumble peered into knotholes that seemed to wink at him, squinted at shimmering mica flecks that danced in the sunlight, and even suspected a particularly round, moss-covered mushroom that had a curious, unblinking spot on its cap. He even asked a grumpy-looking beetle, who just scuttled away muttering about impudent goblins.

‘Aha!’ Tumble suddenly yelped, pointing a grubby finger so forcefully he nearly poked Pickle in the eye. ‘The eye! It’s… it’s a puddle!’

Pickle blinked. And then blinked again, just to be sure his eyesight hadn't been affected by the altitude. It was, indeed, a small, perfectly formed puddle, reflecting the vast, indifferent sky like a tiny, watery mirror. It certainly didn't blink. Not even a little flutter. Tumble, however, was already convinced. He was already digging. He dug with the frantic, uncontainable energy of a badger who’d misplaced his favourite, extra-juicy worm and was absolutely determined to find it, or perhaps a gold coin. He dug until his fingers were sore and his face was streaked with mud from his brow to his chin, giving him the distinguished look of a miniature swamp monster. He found… a single, tarnished button.

‘A button!’ Tumble groaned, throwing his hands up in despair, sending a small flurry of mud in Pickle’s direction. ‘Not even a shiny one! This map is utter rubbish! A complete and utter Gribble-disappointment!’

‘Or,’ Pickle murmured, nudging the forlorn button with his nose, his intelligent eyes twinkling, ‘it’s very specific about what it doesn’t contain. Perhaps the treasure is the journey… or the button itself.’

Tumble scowled. He was about to declare Operation: Magnificent Meal a catastrophic bust, and his tummy was starting to compose a very angry opera, when a thought, bright and shiny as a freshly polished acorn, popped into his head. He looked at the button. He looked at the puddle. He looked at the ‘sighing stone,’ which was now sighing even more dramatically, probably because it was tired of being dug up.

‘Pickle,’ he said, his voice dropping to a low, conspiratorial whisper, the kind you use when planning a raid on the cookie jar. ‘What if the treasure isn’t gold? What if it’s… something else?’ He remembered the dusty little observatories he’d passed, the ones with the gleaming brass telescopes and the intricate charts of the cosmos that looked like tangled spiderwebs. He remembered seeing a sign outside one particularly leaning establishment, it read: ‘The Celestial Curio Shop – Peculiarities for the Perplexed.’ Peculiarities! And what was more peculiar, more perplexing, than a map that led to a button and a puddle?

‘Come on!’ Tumble whispered, scooping up the button and carefully cupping the puddle in a large, sturdy leaf. ‘We’re going to trade!’

They scrambled down the mountain, their descent much faster than their ascent, following the squiggly mule paths with renewed vigour. As dawn began to paint the eastern sky with soft, rosy hues, like a giant artist blending gentle colours, a single, misty tendril curled lazily around a distant bell tower. The tower, still sleepy from its nightly slumber, chimed a single, resonant note. It was a moment of pure, quiet magic, a gentle pause in Tumble’s often chaotic world.

They arrived at the Celestial Curio Shop, a wonky building that leaned precariously to one side, as if it had had one too many star-gazing sessions and was perpetually a little tipsy. Inside, amidst shelves crammed with shimmering stardust, bottled whispers, and what looked suspiciously like a petrified sneeze, a peculiar gnome with spectacles perched on the very tip of his nose, named Professor Sprout (not *that* Professor Sprout, a different one entirely, though equally fond of gardening and peculiar magical ingredients), was polishing a crystal ball that gleamed with captured moonlight.

‘Good day!’ Tumble announced, trying his very best to sound nonchalant, like a goblin who regularly traded in mystical artifacts. ‘I have a… unique item for trade.’ He proudly presented the tarnished button.

Professor Sprout peered at it through his enormous spectacles. ‘Hmm. A genuine Gribble-Button,’ he murmured, his voice like the rustle of dry leaves. ‘Quite rare. Collectors prize these. They say each one holds the echo of a goblin’s boast.’ He then looked at the puddle Tumble had carefully collected in the leaf. ‘And a Whisper-Mountain Dewdrop, caught at the dawn sigh. Fascinating moisture content, and I detect the faintest hint of mountain melancholy.’

Tumble blinked, his ears twitching with hopeful anticipation. ‘So… you’ll give me coins?’ he asked, trying to keep the desperation out of his voice.

Professor Sprout chuckled, a sound like tiny bells tinkling. ‘My dear goblin, this is not merely a shopping list with ambition. These are artifacts! They tell a story! A Gribble-Button! The perfect finishing touch for the waistcoat of any discerning goblin who wishes to impress at the annual sock-swapping convention. And the Dewdrop! For the enchanted garden of any anxious pixie who needs a touch of dawn’s quiet comfort. For these… I shall offer you… one rather hefty coin pouch!’

Tumble practically vibrated with pure, unadulterated joy. He exchanged his treasures – the button and the dewdrop – for a pouch so wonderfully, gloriously full of coins that when he hefted it, it made the most satisfying CLINK-CLANK-CLUNK! sound imaginable. It was the symphony of a well-fed goblin!

‘OH! OH! This is the best part!’ Tumble exclaimed, practically skipping back up the mountain, the coin pouch bouncing merrily against his leg. ‘Great-Uncle Gribble’s map wasn’t wrong, it was just… misunderstood! He probably made a fortune selling ‘peculiarities’ himself! He was a genius! A true, sock-loving, treasure-finding genius!’

Pickle chirped happily, nuzzling Tumble’s ear. He’d known Tumble would figure it out. He always did. And Tumble, in turn, gave Pickle an extra-gentle pat, for being the best, most wisest rat a goblin could ask for.

That night, Tumble and Pickle enjoyed the most magnificent supper of roasted roots that tasted like sunshine, plump, juicy grubs that popped with flavour (and no one dared call them gross!), and a generous slice of berry crumble, all thanks to a map, a button, a puddle, and the resourceful, charming goblin who knew that sometimes, the most valuable treasures aren’t made of gold, but of cleverness, a good friend, and a dash of magnificent misunderstanding. And Pickle? He got an extra-grub. Naturally. Because even a pragmatic rat deserves a reward for putting up with a goblin’s grand ideas!
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
